items.question: How does FF stop the next hidden layer from trivially telling positive from negative data by using the previous layer's activity?

documents.title: The Forward-Forward Algorithm: Some Preliminary Investigations

items.text:
FF blocks the shortcut with **layer normalization**: before a hidden layer's activity vector is passed on as input to the next layer, its length is normalized away.

The paper puts it directly — a single hidden layer can learn goodness, but if its raw activities became the next layer's input, the next layer could just measure the vector's length rather than learn any new features. The fix:

> To prevent this, FF normalizes the length of the hidden vector before using it as input to the next layer… [p. 3](citation:1)

The intuition Hinton gives is length vs. orientation: the activity vector's **length** carries the goodness signal, and only the **orientation** survives normalization and reaches the next layer [p. 3](citation:2). Since normalization removes exactly the information used to compute goodness, the next layer is forced to look at the *relative* activities of the neurons, which normalization leaves unchanged [p. 3](citation:3).

So the answer in one line: each layer's own goodness is computed on the *unnormalized* activity, but what the next layer sees is the *normalized* vector — length removed, orientation kept.

Section 2.1 on page 3 is where this is explained — I've moved the reader there.

items.question: What does the paper report about separating FF's positive and negative phases in time, i.e. doing many updates on positive data and then many on negative data (as in sleep)?

documents.title: The Forward-Forward Algorithm: Some Preliminary Investigations

items.text:
The paper addresses this directly in §5 "Sleep", and the news is mostly negative.

Hinton says that in an early draft he reported it was possible to do many updates on positive data followed by many on self-generated negative data with little loss in performance [p. 9](citation:1). But he now retracts that: he was unable to replicate the result and suspects it was due to a bug [p. 9](citation:2).

With the sum-of-squared-activities goodness function, separating the phases essentially fails in practice:

- Alternating thousands of positive updates then thousands of negative updates only works with a **very low learning rate and extremely high momentum** [p. 9](citation:3).
- He leaves open that a different goodness function might allow the phases to be separated, but says this is unproven and "probably the most important outstanding question about FF as a biological model" [p. 9](citation:4).

So the "sleep" interpretation — positive data while awake, negative data during sleep — is currently **not supported** by the experiments; it is an open question, not an established result. He also notes the contrast with Boltzmann Machines, whose learning rule likewise fails if many positive updates are followed by many negative updates, as would be required if the negative phase were REM sleep [p. 9](citation:5).

As a side thought, he suggests that if phase separation could be made to work, temporarily removing negative-phase updates might mimic the effects of severe sleep deprivation [p. 9](citation:6).

items.question: B and W never communicate directly. How, according to the authors, does information about the fixed random feedback matrix B end up shaping the forward output weights W?

documents.title: Random synaptic feedback weights support error backpropagation for deep learning

items.text:
It's an **indirect, two-step flow** through the hidden layer — B and W never touch each other. Recall the network from the Results: $y = Wh$, with $h = W_0 x$, so $W_0$ is input→hidden and $W$ is hidden→output [p. 3](citation:1).

The update rules are where the asymmetry lives: $W$ is updated exactly as in backprop, $\Delta W \propto e h^\mathsf{T}$, but $W_0$ is updated with the random matrix instead of $W^\mathsf{T}$:

$$\Delta W_0 \propto B e\, x^\mathsf{T}$$

So **B acts directly only on $W_0$**. B's "weight information" enters the network by shaping the hidden-layer weights; those reshaped weights then change the hidden representation $h = W_0 x$, and since $W$ learns from that representation, the influence of B flows forward into $W$ [p. 5](citation:2). The result is that $W$ evolves to align with $B^\mathsf{T}$, at which point $B$ can act *like* $W^\mathsf{T}$ and deliver useful teaching signals to the hidden units.

The authors prove this ordering with a three-phase experiment (Fig. 5c): freeze $W$ while $W_0$ learns and the error barely moves, because the changes are driven by a $B$ not yet aligned with $W^\mathsf{T}$; then freeze $W_0$ while $W$ learns, which is the phase where $W$ aligns with $B^\mathsf{T}$; then learning $W_0$ again finally reduces the error [p. 5](citation:3). In short: **B sculpts $W_0$, $W_0$ sculpts $h$, and $h$ sculpts $W$** — no direct channel between B and W is needed.

items.question: How do the authors measure the cross-entropy loss of the unsupervised SoftHebb network during training, given that the true hidden causes are not available?

documents.title: SoftHebb: Bayesian inference in unsupervised Hebbian soft winner-take-all networks

items.text:
They call their solution the **post-hoc cross-entropy method**, described at the end of §2.9. The core problem is that the true hidden causes $C$ are unknown even when labels $L$ are available:

> It has not been obvious how to correctly measure the loss of an unsupervised WTA network during the learning process, since the ground truth for causes C is often not available, even if labels L are available [p. 10](citation:1)

The trick rests on their theoretical result that SoftHebb's model of the causes implies a model of the labels, $Q(L_l) = \sum_k P(L_l|C_k)Q(C_k)$, and minimizing cross-entropy on one is equivalent to minimizing it on the other (their Eq. 19). So instead of needing the unavailable causes, they measure through the labels — and they replace the unknown causal link $P(L_l|C)$ with a supervised classifier trained on SoftHebb's own outputs.

Their procedure is three-step: (a) train SoftHebb unsupervised; (b) train a supervised classifier on top of SoftHebb's outputs using the labels; then (c) re-run SoftHebb's training with the *same initial weights and same input ordering* as in (a), while measuring the frozen classifier's loss on the evolving representations. That readout curve is the post-hoc cross-entropy of SoftHebb, and by Eq. 19 they infer the cause-level cross-entropy $H_C$ is being minimized too. They validate it empirically in §3.2 / Fig. 4C, where the curve confirms SoftHebb lowers label cross-entropy faster than hard WTA and backpropagation, despite never seeing the labels.

In short: they don't measure against the hidden causes directly — they measure against the available labels through a trained readout, justified by the cause–label equivalence they derived.

failed.quote: Here we introduce a new, simple form of anti-Hebbian plasticity for soft WTA networks, that simply negates SoftHebb\u2019s weight update (Equation (2)) in all neurons except the maximally activated one.
The plasticity defined for a synaptic weight wik from a presynaptic neuron i with activation xi to a neuron k is \u2206w(SoftHebb) ik = \u03b7 \u00b7 yk \u00b7 (xi \u2212uk \u00b7 wik) . (2)

repair.draft:
The authors introduce the anti-Hebbian term as a soft variant, contrasting it with earlier hard-WTA anti-Hebbian rules. In previous work anti-Hebbian plasticity was "applied to the k-th most active neuron" in hard-WTA networks, whereas their new version is, in their words, a "new, simple form of anti-Hebbian plasticity for soft WTA networks, that simply negates SoftHebb's weight update (Equation (2)) in all neurons except the maximally activated one" [p. 5](cite:27 "Here we introduce a new, simple form of anti-Hebbian plasticity for soft WTA networks, that simply negates SoftHebb\u2019s weight update (Equation (2)) in all neurons except the maximally activated one.").

items.question: How did the authors decide how many hidden layers to stack for each dataset?

documents.title: Hebbian Deep Learning Without Feedback

items.text:
The depth isn't chosen per dataset by performance tuning — it follows a fixed **resolution rule** set out in section A.5. Each layer uses stride-2 pooling, which halves each spatial dimension, and they simply stop stacking layers once the output resolution drops to **4×4 or smaller** [p. 17](citation:1). Since that point depends on the input resolution, it yields:

- **MNIST / CIFAR-10** (28×28 / 32×32): 3 convolutional layers
- **STL-10** (96×96): 4 layers
- **ImageNet** at 160×160: 5 layers

Separately, they did tune the **width factor** $f_w$ (how the filter count grows across layers) using CIFAR-10, trying $f_w \in \{1, 2, 4\}$ [p. 17](citation:2) — but the *number* of layers came from the 4×4 stopping rule, not from a search.

items.question: Which paper in my library argues that each MNIST image's true hidden cause is a combination of the digit and a handwriting style, and uses this to show that an unsupervised Hebbian network minimizes cross-entropy with respect to labels it never sees?

documents.title: SoftHebb: Bayesian inference in unsupervised Hebbian soft winner-take-all networks

items.text:
The paper is **SoftHebb: Bayesian inference in unsupervised Hebbian soft winner-take-all networks** (paper 26).

It argues exactly this on page 10: the MNIST labels "do not correspond exactly to the true cause of each example image" — rather, the direct cause is a combination of the digit $L$ with one of many handwriting styles $S$, so $P(C_k) = P(L_l)P(S_s)$ [p. 10](citation:1). From this, the paper shows that minimizing the cross-entropy between the network's implicit label model and the true labels is equivalent to minimizing cross-entropy over the hidden causes $C$ — which SoftHebb does, without ever seeing the labels: "SoftHebb never accesses the labels or any other supervisory signal" [p. 10](citation:2).

So the key chain is: unsupervised SoftHebb minimizes $H_C$ → which implies minimizing $H_L$, the cross-entropy with respect to labels it never sees.

items.question: How does the SDMLP's Top-K activation differ from the k-sparse approach of Makhzani & Frey, which keeps only the k most active units?

documents.title: Sparse Distributed Memory is a Continual Learner

items.text:
The difference is in what happens to the **k surviving neurons**. Makhzani & Frey's k-sparse autoencoder zeroes out everything below the top $k$ but leaves the winners' activations **unchanged**. The SDMLP instead applies a true inhibitory subtraction: it subtracts the $(k{+}1)$-th largest activation from *every* neuron that stays on, so the winners are attenuated rather than kept at their raw values.

In short:

- **Makhzani & Frey (k-sparse autoencoder):** threshold at the $k$-th largest value — the top $k$ keep their exact pre-activation values, everything else is zeroed. [p. 5](citation:1)
- **SDMLP:** computes $I$ = the $(k{+}1)$-th largest activation and applies $a^* = [a - I]^+$. This zeroes the same non-winners (via ReLU), but also *subtracts* $I$ from the $k$ winners, shrinking them. [p. 5](citation:2)

The paper frames this as the difference between a hard "keep or kill" threshold and an inhibitory-interneuron-style competition, and reports the subtraction version gives "a significant boost in continual learning" [p. 5](citation:3). The full update is Eq. (4) on page 5.

items.question: Which optimizer do the authors use to train the SDMLP for continual learning, and why do they avoid Adam and RMSProp?

documents.title: Sparse Distributed Memory is a Continual Learner

items.text:
The authors train the SDMLP with **plain SGD without momentum**.

They avoid Adam and RMSProp because of what they call the **stale momentum problem**: in a sparse Top-K activation setting, an optimizer with a moving average of gradients keeps updating inactive neurons with an out-of-date momentum term, and then explodes the gradient magnitude when a quiescent neuron becomes active again — killing neurons and hurting continual learning. They coin this problem on the grounds that momentum-based optimizers "especially Adam and RMSProp" fail to compute an accurate moving average in the sparse setting [p. 5](citation:1). Their solution is explicitly to drop the momentum term: [p. 5](citation:2).

In Appendix D they report the ordering of results: SGD without momentum removes the problem, and "SGD with momentum works worse than SGD without momentum, but still better than Adam or RMSProp" [p. 36](citation:3). This matches the ablation table, where SGD reaches 0.63 validation accuracy versus 0.23 for Adam and 0.20 for RMSProp [p. 9](citation:4).

items.question: In the spiking LIF network, why do the authors switch off learning for a period after each change from one input pattern to the next?

documents.title: Biologically plausible deep learning — But how far can we go with shallow networks?

items.text: They pause learning because right after a pattern switch the network goes through a **transient phase** in which its activity is not yet a clean response to the new input. During that phase the spikes still carry a mix of the previous pattern and the current one, but the STDP rule is designed to work on activity driven by a *single* pattern. The authors report that without disabling learning through these transients the networks never reached a low test error [p. 7](citation:1). In the methods they specify the switch-off window as a duration of $T_\mathrm{trans} = 4\tau_m$, chosen because the noise introduced by the transients was found to deteriorate learning [p. 11](citation:2). During testing, learning is shut off permanently.

This is not surprising, since in this phase the network activities carry information both about the previously presented pattern and the current one, but the learning rule is designed for network activities in response to a single input pattern.

items.question: Based on their weight-perturbation test on a single-game DQN, what do the authors identify as the chief limitation of their EWC implementation?

documents.title: Overcoming catastrophic forgetting in neural networks

items.text:
They identify the chief limitation as **under-estimating parameter uncertainty**.

The clue came from the nullspace perturbation: in theory, perturbing weights the Fisher information says are unimportant should leave performance untouched, but empirically it hurt the agent just as much as perturbing the inverse-Fisher directions. The authors read this as over-confidence in their importance estimates:

> it is therefore likely that the chief limitation of the current implementation is that it under-estimates parameter uncertainty. [p. 6](citation:1)

In other words, their diagonal-Fisher approximation marks some parameters as safely ignorable when they actually matter, so EWC lets those weights drift more than it should.

items.question: How do the authors measure the overlap between two tasks' Fisher information matrices?

documents.title: Overcoming catastrophic forgetting in neural networks

items.text:
They measure it as **1 − Fréchet distance between the two normalized Fisher matrices**. The procedure [p. 13](citation:1) is:

1. Compute each task's Fisher, $F_1$ and $F_2$.
2. Normalize each to unit trace: $\hat F_1$, $\hat F_2$.
3. Compute the Fréchet distance (a metric on positive-semidefinite matrices):

$$d^2(\hat F_1, \hat F_2) = \tfrac{1}{2}\operatorname{tr}\!\big(\hat F_1 + \hat F_2 - 2(\hat F_1 \hat F_2)^{1/2}\big) = \tfrac{1}{2}\|\hat F_1^{1/2} - \hat F_2^{1/2}\|_F^2$$

This distance is bounded between 0 and 1, and they define **overlap = 1 − d²**, so [p. 13](citation:2) a value of 0 means non-overlapping weights, and 1 means the Fishers are proportional ($F_1 = \alpha F_2$).

In the cerebellar mapping, each **granule cell** is the hidden neuron, with its dendrites as the address vector and its synapses onto Purkinje cells as the stored values: [p. 17](citation:2). The strength of each Purkinje-cell contact records a single element of that stored vector: [p. 17](citation:3).

Crucially for your question, the continual-learning success is "organic" to the architecture — the paper states it does not require any task labels, task boundaries, or memory replay: [p. 2](citation:4).
